history.content: How many types of bonds are there?

Bond MFs and ETFs come in many flavors. One way to categorize them is by type: corporate, government (gilt/sovereign), money market (short-term, overnight lending, etc.), and government-backed bonds. The ETFs and MFs that invest in these are also of different types.

An Exchange-Traded Fund (ETF) is a unique type of mutual fund that is traded on the stock exchange, similar to how individual stocks are bought and sold. To invest in an ETF, you purchase it through a stockbroker, just as you would with a regular stock. From an accounting perspective, an ETF functions essentially like a stock and can be treated as just another stock in your investment portfolio.
An ETF does not focus on tracking any single individual stock; rather, it is a marketable security that follows an index, a commodity, bonds, or a group of assets, much like an index fund. ETFs offer high liquidity, making them beneficial for active traders, and they provide a straightforward investment option for individuals who may not meet the minimum balance requirements of traditional mutual funds, where transactions are settled at the end of the trading day.
What do they have in common with mutual funds?

Mutual funds and ETFs (Exchange-Traded Funds) are very similar in nature. Both can serve a variety of purposes and have different policies, which makes it essential to understand the prospectus before investing. Since both mutual funds and ETFs offer a wide range of options, discussing management, assets, or expenses when comparing the two can lead to inaccuracies. In essence, ETFs and mutual funds share many similarities and provide essentially the same service to investors, with only minimal differences.
One way to think about it is to say that an ETF is a type of mutual fund that comes with unique features not typically found in traditional mutual funds. For example, bond ETFs offer another means of investing in bond mutual funds. An ETF allows you to trade shares similarly to stocks, enabling transactions in small share increments.

Do I need to get one?

Most individuals do not require a personal financial advisor. If you are about to enter the workforce, consider focusing your discretionary investments on index funds you can hold for the long term. If you do not have the time or interest to manage your investments, hiring a financial advisor may be beneficial. There are many fee-based financial advisors available who offer these services. evidence.text: "Since as you say, an LLC is a pass-through entity, you will be making income in the U.S. when you sell to U.S. customers.  And so you will need to file the appropriate personal tax forms in the US.  As well as potentially in one or more States.  The US government does not register LLCs.  The various States do.  So you'll be dealing with Oregon, Wisconsin, Wyoming, one of those for the LLC registration.  You will also need to have a registered agent in the State.  That is a big deal since the entire point of forming an LLC is to add a liability shield.  You would lose the liability shield by not maintaining the business formalities.   Generally nations aim to tax income made in their nation, and many decline to tax income that you've already paid taxes on in another nation.  A key exception: If money is taxed by the U.S. it may also be taxed by one of the States.  Two States won't tax the same dollar. Registering an LLC in one State does not mean you'll pay state taxes there.

LLC is not a federal tax designation.  It's a state-level organization. Your LLC can elect to be treated as a partnership, a disregarded entity (i.e., just report the taxes in your individual income tax), or as an S-Corp for federal tax purposes. If you have elected S-Corp, I expect that all the S-Corp rules will apply, as well as any state-level LLC rules that may apply.   Disclaimer: I'm not 100% familiar with S-corp rules, so I can't evaluate whether the statements you made about proportional payouts are correct.
